content: FABP1, also known as Fatty Acid-Binding Protein 1, is a human gene that encodes the protein product FABP1. This protein is frequently referred to as liver-type fatty acid-binding protein (LFABP). It is predominantly expressed in the liver, where it plays a critical role in the binding, transport, and metabolism of long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs), endocannabinoids, phytocannabinoids, and other hydrophobic molecules. Its role in binding synthetic cannabinoid receptor (CBR) agonists and antagonists is less pronounced. Altered expression of FABP1 has been associated with metabolic conditions, including obesity. Discovery Fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs) were first identified in 1972 through experiments using radiolabeled oleate to detect a soluble fatty acid carrier in enterocytes, which are responsible for intestinal absorption of LCFAs. Since then, ten members of the FABP family have been identified in the human genome. Nine of these (FABP1–9) are well-characterized, while a tenth member (FABP12) was more recently discovered. Each FABP is associated with specific organs or tissues in the body, where they facilitate fatty acid uptake, transport, and metabolism. Gene Location The human FABP1 gene is located on the short (p) arm of chromosome 2, spanning base pairs 88,122,982 to 88,128,131. Protein Structure FABP1 has a unique structure compared to other members of the FABP family, enabling it to bind multiple ligands simultaneously. It also possesses a larger solvent-accessible core, which allows for the binding of a more diverse range of substrates. The portal hypothesis has been proposed to explain the binding mechanism of FABPs. According to this hypothesis, fatty acids enter the solvent-accessible region of the protein through a dynamic area formed by α-helix II and the loops between βC-βD and βE-βF. Once inside, the fatty acid is bound within the protein cavity for transport. Function FABPs are a family of small, highly conserved cytoplasmic proteins involved in the binding of LCFAs. FABP1 is abundantly expressed in the human liver, where it constitutes 7–11% of the total cytosolic protein. It is also found in the intestine, kidney, pancreas, stomach, and lung. FABP1 is unique in its ability to bind a wide range of hydrophobic ligands, including bilirubin, monoglycerides, bile acids, and fatty acyl-CoA. It is thought to play a significant role in preventing cytotoxicity by binding heme, fatty acids, and other potentially toxic molecules when they are unbound. Mutations A missense mutation in exon 3 of the human FABP1 gene has been identified, involving a substitution of alanine to threonine (Ala to Thr), resulting in the T94A variant. Carriers of this single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) exhibit higher baseline plasma-free fatty acid levels, lower body mass index (BMI), and smaller waist circumference. The T94A mutation has also been linked to metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Protein Expression Suppression Studies in mice have investigated the effects of suppressing the FABP1 gene. When subjected to high-fat or high-cholesterol diets, mice with suppressed FABP1 expression showed significant impacts on metabolic regulation and weight gain. Increased Levels in Obesity Research in Chinese young adults has demonstrated a strong correlation between serum FABP1 levels and lipid profiles, body measurements, and homeostatic parameters. Individuals with higher BMI and insulin resistance exhibited elevated serum FABP1 levels, particularly those with central adiposity. This increase is thought to represent a compensatory upregulation of the protein in response to the high metabolic stress associated with obesity. Alternatively, obesity may induce resistance to the actions of FABP1, leading to its compensatory upregulation. Disease Marker Elevated levels of urinary and serum FABP1 have been shown to be effective biomarkers for detecting intestinal ischemia, progressive end-stage renal failure, and ischemic damage caused by renal transplantation or cardiac bypass surgery.
